lead: A linear system is a list of straight-line conditions that must all hold at the same time. Writing it as Ax = b puts every coefficient into one matrix A, the unknowns into one column x, and the right-hand numbers into one column b. That split is useful, because the pattern of solutions depends on A and b, not on the letters x, y, z. Engineers solve mesh currents this way, price puzzles reduce to it, and every elimination method from Gaussian elimination onwards begins by writing Ax = b.
prereq: You need: multiplying a matrix by a column vector, and plotting a straight line from ax + by = c.

blocks.text: A linear equation has no squares, no products of unknowns, no roots of unknowns. 2x + 3y − z = 7 is linear. xy = 6 and x² + y = 1 are not. A linear system is m such equations in n unknowns, all required to be true together.

blocks.where: A is the m×n coefficient matrix: m rows, one per equation; n columns, one per unknown. The entry aᵢⱼ multiplies xⱼ in equation i. x is the n×1 column of unknowns. b is the m×1 column of right-hand sides.

blocks.text: The row index i counts equations, the column index j counts unknowns. Row 2 of A holds the coefficients of x₁, …, xₙ in the second equation. Multiplying A by x gives one number per equation — the left-hand side — and each must equal the matching entry of b.

Glue b to the right of A, after a vertical bar, to get the augmented matrix [A|b]. It stores every number in the problem, so the equations can be rebuilt from it. Row moves in elementary row operations act on the whole of [A|b], the b column included.
If b = 0 the system is homogeneous. If b ≠ 0 it is non-homogeneous. Homogeneous systems are special: x = 0, every unknown zero, always satisfies A0 = 0. That is called the trivial solution.

blocks.where: the 0 on the right is the m×1 zero column; x = 0 means x₁ = x₂ = ⋯ = xₙ = 0.

blocks.text: So a homogeneous system is never short of a solution. The real question is whether other solutions exist, and that depends on the coefficients. x + y = 0 with x − y = 0 forces x = 0, y = 0 only. But x + y = 0 with 2x + 2y = 0 accepts (1, −1), (2, −2) and every multiple — a whole line of non-trivial solutions.
A non-homogeneous system can fail outright: x + y = 2 and x + y = 5 cannot both hold.
Two words carry the verdict. A system with at least one solution is consistent. A system with no solution is inconsistent. Every homogeneous system is consistent.
For n = 2 each equation ax + by = c, with a and b not both zero, is a straight line, so solving the system means finding points that lie on all the lines at once. Three things can happen.

items: The lines meet at one point: one solution, consistent. x + y = 3 and x − y = 1 meet at (2, 1).
The lines are parallel: no solution, inconsistent. x + y = 3 and x + y = 5 never meet.
The lines coincide: infinitely many solutions, consistent. x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 6 are the same line.

blocks.text: For n = 3 each equation is a plane, and planes can miss each other, touch at a point, meet along a line, or sit on top of each other. The three outcomes do not change with size; only the pictures get harder to draw.

This is why the matrix form matters. The coefficient matrix A, not the letters x, y, z, fixes the shape of the solution set. Which of the three outcomes you get is settled by rank, as the chapter on rank and consistency shows.

figure.caption: The chain from a word problem to the augmented matrix. Only [A|b] moves on to row operations, because it keeps the right-hand numbers beside the coefficients.

spec.title: From a problem to an augmented matrix
spec.aria: A left-to-right flow from a word problem to linear equations, then to the matrix form Ax = b, then to the augmented matrix [A|b].

examples.question: For the system x + y + z = 6, x − y + 2z = 5, 2x + y − z = 1, write it in the form Ax = b, form the augmented matrix, and check whether x = 1, y = 2, z = 3 is a solution.
steps: Count: m = 3 equations and n = 3 unknowns, so A is 3×3, x is 3×1 and b is 3×1.
Read coefficients row by row. Row 1: x + y + z = 6 gives coefficients 1, 1, 1 and b₁ = 6.
Row 2: x − y + 2z = 5 gives coefficients 1, −1, 2 and b₂ = 5.
Row 3: 2x + y − z = 1 gives coefficients 2, 1, −1 and b₃ = 1.
Check equation 1: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, which equals b₁ = 6. Holds.
Check equation 2: 1 − 2 + 2(3) = 1 − 2 + 6 = 5, which equals b₂ = 5. Holds.
Check equation 3: 2(1) + 2 − 3 = 2 + 2 − 3 = 1, which equals b₃ = 1. Holds.
All three equations are satisfied, so (1, 2, 3) is a solution and the system is consistent.
examples.answer: A = [[1, 1, 1], [1, −1, 2], [2, 1, −1]], b = [6, 5, 1]ᵗ, the augmented matrix is [1 1 1 | 6; 1 −1 2 | 5; 2 1 −1 | 1], and x = 1, y = 2, z = 3 is a solution since the three left-hand sides come out as 6, 5 and 1.
examples.output: Left-hand sides at (1, 2, 3): 6, 5, 1 — matching b₁, b₂, b₃.

traps: Assuming every homogeneous system has only x = 0. The trivial solution always exists; extra solutions depend on the coefficients, not on the word 'homogeneous'.
A row operation must act on the whole augmented row, including the b column. Changing A alone silently changes the solution set.
Reading 'non-homogeneous' as 'inconsistent'. It only means b ≠ 0; such a system may have one solution, infinitely many, or none.
Confusing consistent with 'has a unique solution'. Consistent means at least one solution, so the infinite case counts too.
Writing A as m×n and then writing b as a row. b is a column, m×1, and it becomes the extra (n+1)-th column of [A|b].

quiz.q: Define a homogeneous and a non-homogeneous linear system.
quiz.a: A system Ax = b is homogeneous if b = 0, that is every right-hand side is zero. It is non-homogeneous if b ≠ 0, that is at least one right-hand side is non-zero.

quiz.q: What is the trivial solution, and which system always has it?
quiz.a: The trivial solution is x₁ = x₂ = ⋯ = xₙ = 0. Every homogeneous system has it, because A0 = 0.

quiz.q: Why is a homogeneous system never inconsistent?
quiz.a: Setting every unknown to zero makes each left-hand side zero, which equals the zero right-hand side. So the all-zero column is always a solution, and a system with at least one solution is consistent by definition.

quiz.q: Why do we keep the augmented matrix [A|b] instead of working with A alone?
quiz.a: A alone stores only the coefficients; the right-hand numbers are needed to recover the equations and to detect an inconsistency such as 0 = 5. [A|b] holds every number of the problem, so row operations on it preserve the full solution set.

quiz.q: Write 3x − y = 4 and x + 2y = 5 in the form Ax = b and give the augmented matrix.
Check whether x = 1, y = 2 solves 2x + 3y = 8 and x − y = −1.
quiz.a: Equation 1: 2(1) + 3(2) = 2 + 6 = 8, equals 8. Equation 2: 1 − 2 = −1, equals −1. Both hold, so (1, 2) is a solution and the system is consistent.

quiz.q: Two systems share the coefficient matrix A = [1 1] and each starts as a single equation, x + y = 3 in one and x + y = 5 in the other. A second equation is added to each. Can one system be consistent and the other inconsistent? Give the second equation in each case.
quiz.a: Both single-equation systems are consistent as they stand, since one equation in two unknowns has a whole line of solutions. Adding a second equation can change that. Add x + y = 3 to the first system (x + y = 3): the two equations coincide, infinitely many solutions, consistent. Add x + y = 6 to the second system (x + y = 5): the two lines are parallel and distinct, no solution, inconsistent. The same A = [1 1] supports different verdicts because the b column differs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems in circuit simulation, structural design and recommendation models often have thousands or millions of unknowns, and A is mostly zeros; such sparse systems are never solved by hand elimination. Instead they go to iterative solvers that start from a guess and improve it, or to matrix factorizations such as LU that are reused for many different b. Least-squares problems, where no exact solution exists at all, are handled in Unit 5. Search next for 'sparse linear systems', 'iterative solvers' and 'conjugate gradient'.
